label: CAT(k) Spaces
notes: This unit opens part two of the course and turns the comparison philosophy into a precise definition. We bound curvature from above by comparing real geodesic triangles against flat or curved model triangles. The slogan to keep in mind is that a CAT(k) space has triangles no fatter than the model.

label: Model Spaces M_k
notes: Before comparing anything we fix the yardsticks. The model spaces are the sphere of curvature k, the Euclidean plane at curvature zero, and the hyperbolic plane scaled by negative k. The diameter of M_k is finite exactly when k is positive, which forces a size restriction on the triangles we may compare.

label: Geodesic Triangles
notes: A geodesic triangle is three points joined by three chosen geodesic segments. We insist the space be geodesic so segments exist, and we record the side lengths. These three numbers are the only data the comparison construction uses, so the triangle is summarised entirely by its perimeter and edge lengths.

label: Comparison Triangle
notes: Given a triangle in the space we build a triangle in the model with identical side lengths. In Euclidean and hyperbolic models such a triangle always exists and is unique up to isometry; in the spherical model we additionally need the perimeter below twice the model diameter. Each real point gets a comparison point on the matching edge.

label: The CAT(k) Inequality
notes: Here is the defining condition. For every pair of points on the real triangle, the distance between them is at most the distance between their comparison points in the model. Triangles in a CAT(k) space are therefore thinner than the model triangles of the same side lengths. This single inequality drives the entire theory.

label: Thin versus Fat
notes: The picture contrasts a non-positively curved triangle, whose chord falls inside the flat comparison chord, with a positively curved triangle that bulges outward. Thin means each interior chord is shorter than its model counterpart; fat means longer. CAT(0) captures the thin regime that Alexandrov identified as non-positive curvature.

label: CAT(0) = Non-Positive Curvature
notes: Setting k to zero gives the central case. A CAT(0) space is geodesic and satisfies the comparison against the Euclidean plane. This is Alexandrov's synthetic definition of curvature bounded above by zero, requiring no smoothness. Trees, Euclidean buildings, and products of CAT(0) spaces all qualify and inherit strong convexity properties.

label: Convexity of the Metric
notes: An equivalent face of the same condition is convexity. In a CAT(0) space the distance function between two geodesics is a convex function of the parameter, so geodesics between nearby points stay close. Convexity gives uniqueness of geodesics and the contraction onto convex subsets that later powers fixed-point theorems.

label: The Law of Cosines Bound
notes: The comparison distance can be computed by the model law of cosines. Writing the inequality at the midpoint yields a numerical test on three side lengths and a median, turning a geometric statement into arithmetic. This is exactly the check the notebook samples on a tree-like triangle to confirm the Euclidean comparison numerically.

label: The CN Inequality
notes: Bruhat and Tits packaged the midpoint case as the courbure negative inequality. It bounds the squared distance from a point to a midpoint by averaging the squared distances to the endpoints minus a quarter of the squared edge. For complete spaces the CN inequality is equivalent to the full CAT(0) condition.

label: Four-Point and Reshetnyak
notes: Several equivalent characterizations exist. The four-point condition tests comparison on quadruples; the Reshetnyak gluing and perimeter conditions let us assemble CAT(0) spaces from pieces. Each repackages thinness in a form convenient for a different proof, and all coincide for complete geodesic spaces.

label: Local Bounds and Monotonicity
notes: Curvature bounded above by k locally means every point has a CAT(k) neighbourhood. Comparison is monotone in the bound: a CAT(k) space is automatically CAT(k') for any larger k', since the model triangles only grow fatter. We close by previewing how local bounds globalize under completeness and simple connectivity.
